rule: Never set a Worker secret by passing its value as a command argument, by echoing it into a pipe, or by printing it for a human to copy. Generate it in-process, write it to wrangler's STDIN, hand it off via the clipboard, and display only a masked form. Verify by probing the route for a 200, never by rendering the value back. Two exceptions, both required to be commented where they occur: handing the URL to a browser (no stdin path exists, and the browser holds it in argv and history regardless -- must be opt-out), and a mode-600 file when no clipboard exists (access-controlled, unlike scrollback).
reason: All three obvious ways to set a secret defeat the reason for having a separate credential. A value passed as argv is visible in the process list to every other user on the machine for the lifetime of the call, and lands in shell history. An echoed value lands in shell history too. A printed value lands in terminal scrollback, in any screen-share or screenshot, and in the transcript of any coding agent that ran the command. That last route is measured, not theoretical: this project's own README documents connector URLs found in ~54 occurrences across 13 local session transcripts on a single machine, none pasted deliberately. VIEW_TOKEN exists precisely so a read-only viewer is not also a write credential; leaking it during setup gives back the separation the design bought. The exceptions are narrow on purpose: each was reached only after confirming no stdin-shaped alternative exists, and each is strictly less exposed than the scrollback it replaces.
triggering_incident: PR #7 shipped the /view route but left setting VIEW_TOKEN as a manual step. The first instinct was to generate the token in the assistant's session and run wrangler directly, which would have written the value into the session transcript -- the exact leak channel the README already quantifies. scripts/set-view-token.ps1 moved generation onto the operator's machine at run time, so no participant in the conversation ever observes the value, and the script still cannot be run by an agent without reintroducing the leak.
enforced_by: scripts/set-view-token.ps1 and scripts/set-view-token.sh -- audit every line mentioning the token or full URL; the only permitted sinks are the wrangler stdin pipe, mask derivation, clipboard, the browser handoff, and the mode-600 fallback file

rule: In Windows PowerShell 5.1, never use 2>&1 on a native command while $ErrorActionPreference is 'Stop'. Route native calls through a helper that drops the preference to 'Continue' for the duration of the call and restores it in a finally block.
reason: 5.1 does not merely merge streams for a native command: it wraps each stderr line in an ErrorRecord, and under 'Stop' the first record is a terminating error. The exit code is irrelevant -- a process that returns 0 still kills the script if it wrote a single line to stderr. Tools that print progress, banners, or update notices to stderr are therefore fatal to any script that redirects them, and the failure is deeply misleading: the error text shown is the tool's own benign warning, so it reads as the tool having failed rather than as a redirection bug in the caller.
triggering_incident: set-view-token.ps1 died before wrangler ever ran. The terminating error was an npm notice -- "the following package was not found and will be installed" -- a warning, not a failure. Because the message named npm, the obvious reading was that npm had broken; the actual cause was 2>&1 in the caller. Reproduced deterministically, then fixed with an Invoke-Wrangler helper and re-verified against wrangler triggers deploy --dry-run, which does write WARNING to stderr and now survives.
enforced_by: scripts/set-view-token.ps1::Invoke-Wrangler -- every wrangler invocation must go through it; a bare '& npx wrangler ... 2>&1' in that file is the violation

rule: A runnable command handed to someone must assume nothing about their shell or their working directory. Use forward slashes even on Windows, and either an absolute path or an explicit cd -- never a bare npm run, and never a backslash path.
reason: Two failure modes, and both look like a broken program rather than a bad instruction. (1) Backslash is an escape character in bash -- Git Bash, WSL, and the shell behind most run-this buttons -- so scripts\set-view-token.cmd collapses to scriptsset-view-token.cmd and reports command not found, naming a file nobody wrote. (2) npm run requires the repo as cwd; from one directory up it emits npm error enoent Could not read package.json, which PowerShell then wraps in a NativeCommandError whose first line is 'At line:1 char:1'. That header mentions no directory and no package.json, so it reads as the script having crashed. In both cases the program never executes, so there is no output and no log, and every diagnostic that assumes it ran is chasing nothing.
triggering_incident: Four rounds were spent debugging set-view-token 'failing' -- adding a dry-run mode, a self-writing log, and a trap -- before anyone checked whether it was running. It never was. The user's shell sat in C:\Users\jarms\repos while the agent's tools defaulted into the repo, so no reproduction attempt could ever hit it. The tell was the missing log file: the transcript starts near the top of the script, so its absence meant execution never began. The error was only found by redirecting output to a file and then searching the filesystem for where that file actually landed -- which is what revealed the cwd.
enforced_by: npm run set-view-token in package.json scripts -- the documented entry point; verified from both bash and PowerShell

rule: Never test a PowerShell Read-Host result directly against -match or -notmatch, and never gate on [Environment]::UserInteractive. Cast to [string] first, and detect 'nobody can answer' with [Console]::IsInputRedirected. A confirmation must fail closed.
reason: Two independent ways this fails open. (1) Read-Host returns $null at EOF, and $null -notmatch 'pattern' evaluates to EMPTY rather than $true, so the natural guard is falsy and execution falls through into the action it was meant to gate. Casting to [string] turns $null into the empty string, which the regex correctly fails to match. (2) [Environment]::UserInteractive reports only whether the process has a window station. It stays TRUE with stdin on a pipe, a file, or NUL, so a guard written against it never fires at all -- it is dead code that looks like protection. [Console]::IsInputRedirected is the signal that actually answers 'is anything attached to answer this prompt'. A script that then blocks forever on Read-Host is worse than one that errors: there is no output to read and nothing to report.
triggering_incident: set-view-token.ps1 guarded replacing VIEW_TOKEN behind a Replace it? [y/N] prompt. A captured non-interactive dry run printed the warning and continued straight to the install step, with no prompt and no cancelled anywhere in the output. The first fix added a UserInteractive check, which was itself dead code -- proven later when set-cambium-url.ps1 used the same guard and hung forever on Read-Host instead of refusing. Only the [string] cast was ever doing any work. Both are now in place, verified by piping empty stdin: the script refuses, and -Yes still proceeds.
enforced_by: scripts/set-view-token.ps1 and scripts/set-cambium-url.ps1 -- pipe empty stdin to either; they must refuse or read from stdin, never block and never fall through

rule: Never confirm a deploy with `gh run list --limit 1`. Filter by workflow (`--workflow=deploy.yml`) and check that the run's headSha matches the commit you expect. A repo with CI and Deploy workflows returns whichever finished last, which is usually CI.
reason: The unfiltered list is ordered by recency across ALL workflows. CI is faster than Deploy, so it almost always finishes first and appears at the top. Reading that as the deploy result reports success while the deploy is still running or has already failed. The failure is silent and durable: the code is merged, main looks correct, tests pass, and every later diagnosis proceeds on the false premise that the running Worker matches the source. Confirming the headSha as well catches the second version of the same mistake, where the right workflow succeeded but for an earlier commit.
triggering_incident: cambium-remote's /status route was merged, tested, and reported as deployed on the strength of `gh run list --limit 1` returning completed/success. That was the CI run. The Deploy run had failed on the same commit because CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN and CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID are empty in that repo's GitHub secrets, so the route was never live. The user then ran the setup script, which installed STATUS_TOKEN on cambium-remote, polled the route, got 404 six times, and correctly refused to wire the consumer -- leaving an orphaned token and a wasted round trip. External probing could not have caught it either: the route 404s a wrong token before checking the method, so an absent route and a present one are indistinguishable from outside by design.
enforced_by: gh run list --workflow=deploy.yml --json headSha,conclusion -- compare headSha against git rev-parse HEAD

rule: Never verify a Cloudflare secret immediately after setting it. `wrangler secret put` creates a new Worker version and rolls it out, so for up to a minute some edges still serve the previous version holding the previous value. Poll for at least 60 seconds, and never let the failure message assert a single cause.
reason: A secret change is a deployment, not a database write. Until the new version reaches a given edge, requests there authenticate against the OLD secret, so a correct new token legitimately returns 404 for a while. A short verification window therefore reports a wrong-credential failure for a credential that is correct, and the natural next step -- redeploying, regenerating, or blaming the route -- chases a problem that does not exist. The message matters as much as the timeout: asserting one cause ("it has not been deployed") is confidently wrong half the time, and a wrong diagnosis printed by the tool itself is followed for far longer than no diagnosis at all.
triggering_incident: connect-cambium.ps1 installed STATUS_TOKEN on cambium-remote and polled the status route six times over 18 seconds. All six returned 404 and it refused to wire the consumer, printing "it has not been redeployed since the /status route was added". That was true on the first run and false on the second, after the deploy had already been fixed -- so the second failure sent the diagnosis back to a solved problem. wrangler tail proved the route was live and correct on the deployed version, logging route "/status/***" and surface "status"; the 404s were the previous version still serving during rollout. An earlier tail run that captured nothing looked like proof the route was absent, and was only tail not having finished connecting before the request went out.
enforced_by: scripts/connect-cambium.ps1 -- the verification loop must allow at least 60s and its failure text must list causes in likelihood order, not assert one

rule: A Worker cannot reach another Worker by fetching its workers.dev hostname. Use a service binding. Declare it in BOTH the top-level and the named-environment section, since named environments inherit nothing.
reason: Cloudflare does not route a Worker subrequest to a workers.dev host: the edge answers 404 and the target Worker never executes. From the calling side that is byte-identical to the target rejecting the credential, so the obvious diagnosis is a wrong or unpropagated token, and every fix aimed there is aimed at nothing. The only signal that distinguishes them is the absence of ANY request in the target's own logs. A service binding dispatches in-process -- no DNS, TLS, or egress -- and the request still arrives at the target's normal handler and is still checked against its secret, so the binding replaces the transport and changes nothing about authorization. Keep a plain-fetch fallback for a target on a custom domain, which is routable, or one in another account where no binding can exist.
triggering_incident: The Knowledge panel reported "http 404" with a STATUS_TOKEN that was verifiably correct on both Workers -- the setup script had polled the same URL from the operator's machine and got 200 with counts before installing it. Three rounds went into token propagation and rotation timing before wrangler tail on cambium-remote showed ZERO requests arriving, which proved the call was never reaching it. Adding [[services]] fixed it immediately. The binding then exposed a second layer: with the call finally arriving, it timed out every time, because cambium's status does a GitHub discovery scan across every repo under TEAM_OWNER and the budget was 2500ms -- and that fetch was running on EVERY home page load, not just the tab that renders it.
enforced_by: wrangler.toml -- [[services]] and [[env.production.services]] binding CAMBIUM; vitest.config.ts must stub it or miniflare refuses to start and the whole suite dies

rule: Nothing that names another Worker, another account, or a pinned resource id may appear in the TOP-LEVEL wrangler.toml. That config is what the Deploy to Cloudflare button runs, in an account that has none of those things. Put it under [env.production], and remember named environments inherit nothing.
reason: The top-level profile exists so a stranger's one-click deploy provisions its own resources: the D1 binding deliberately omits database_id for exactly this reason. A service binding is the opposite kind of declaration -- it names a target by name, and Cloudflare rejects the deploy when that Worker does not exist in the deploying account. So a top-level [[services]] breaks the self-host path for everyone except the maintainer, and breaks it at the button, before the deployer has any context for the error. The inheritance direction compounds it: named environments inherit NOTHING, so a binding placed only at the top level is also silently absent from the env CI actually deploys. Both halves have to be got right, and they fail in opposite directions.
triggering_incident: The CAMBIUM service binding needed to reach cambium-remote was added to both the top level and [env.production]. It worked for the maintainer and would have failed every one-click self-host deploy, because no other account has a Worker called cambium-remote. It was caught only while writing the README's installation section -- reading the setup back as a stranger is what surfaced it, not any test, since the test suite and the maintainer deploy both pass with the binding present.
enforced_by: wrangler.toml -- the top-level profile must declare no [[services]] and no database_id; [env.production] carries both

rule: Never emit or run a bare `wrangler deploy` for a repo that declares named environments. Always pass --env explicitly. Any tool that generates a deploy command must refuse to proceed when environments exist and none was named.
reason: A bare deploy targets the TOP-LEVEL config, and in these repos the top level is the self-host profile: it omits database_id on purpose so Cloudflare auto-provisions a fresh D1 for each one-click deployer. Running it against the maintainer's Worker therefore rebinds a live, populated Worker to a brand-new EMPTY database. Nothing errors, nothing warns, and the deploy reports success -- the data is still in the old database but the Worker no longer points at it, so the failure presents as total data loss. The blast radius is maximal and the signal is zero, which is why the generating tool has to fail closed rather than warn.
triggering_incident: install-deploy-hook.ps1 was written for cambium-remote, which has no named environments, so it emitted a bare `wrangler deploy`. It was then pointed at context-keeper-remote to "also cover this repo" -- which does keep its real deployment under [env.production]. The hook installed cleanly and would have bound the live Worker to an empty D1 on the next push, with 34 projects and 301 decisions in the real database. It was removed before any push and the instance verified intact, but nothing in the tooling would have stopped it; the installer now refuses when environments exist and -Env was not given, and refuses an -Env that does not appear in wrangler.toml.
enforced_by: scripts/install-deploy-hook.ps1 -- run it against a repo with [env.*] and no -Env; it must write no hook and must name the environments it found
